summary: Describes the minimal properties an IP Encapsulating Security Payload implementation needs to stay interoperable with standard ESP in RFC 4303. It is not meant to replace ESP, but to allow optimized implementations for constrained environments. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A full toolbox is heavy for tiny devices. This says which tools they can leave out and still work with everyone who has the full box.

questions: how to implement esp on constrained devices
what features can be skipped in esp
how to generate sequence numbers efficiently
subtitle: Which features of IP Encapsulating Security Payload can be left out on constrained devices.

tldr.problem: Full IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) implementations include many features and require significant computational resources. Constrained devices like IoT sensors have limited memory, battery, and processing power, and cannot afford the overhead of a complete ESP stack.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines the minimal features an ESP implementation must have to remain interoperable with standard ESP. It identifies which optional checks can be skipped, how to generate sequence numbers without wearing out flash storage, and how to optimize for battery-constrained devices.
tldr.outcome: Constrained devices can implement a simpler version of ESP that works with standard implementations while saving code size, reducing flash writes, and extending battery life.

today: RFC 9333 is an Informational RFC published in January 2023. It is not a standard that updates or replaces RFC 4303, but rather provides guidance for implementations in constrained environments. It remains the current reference for minimal ESP on IoT and embedded devices.

sections.title: What Is Minimal ESP
sections.content:
ESP is the Encapsulating Security Payload protocol, part of the IPsec suite. It protects IP traffic by encrypting the payload, authenticating it, and providing anti-replay protection. A full ESP implementation can be complex and resource-heavy, with features optimized for general-purpose operating systems.

Constrained devices—such as IoT sensors running on battery—need a minimal version. This RFC does not create a new protocol; rather, it describes which features of the standard ESP (RFC 4303) are optional and how to implement them efficiently on devices with limited flash memory, constrained power, and infrequent network activity.

The goal is interoperability: a minimal ESP implementation must work seamlessly with standard ESP implementations, even though it cuts out features that full implementations may use.
sections.plainLanguage: It is the same security protocol, just with less fancy stuff for tiny computers. A thermometer in your house does not need every security feature a bank's network does.

sections.title: Security Parameters and Identifiers
sections.content:
An ESP packet includes several mandatory fields: a Security Parameters Index (SPI) that identifies which security agreement applies, a sequence number (SN) to prevent replay attacks, encrypted payload data, padding, and an integrity check value (ICV).

For the SPI, a standard implementation generates random 32-bit values. A constrained device may use a simpler scheme—for example, deriving the SPI from memory addresses or a counter—since the SPI is only used to identify incoming traffic and each device controls its own inbound SPI space. However, any non-random scheme carries privacy risks: an observer could infer the device type or firmware version from SPI patterns.

For the sequence number, a full implementation increments a counter with each packet. Constrained devices can instead derive the SN from a timer or clock, reducing the need to write to flash memory after each transmission. This saves battery and prolongs flash storage life.
sections.plainLanguage: The SPI is a label that says 'this is from that device.' A full system picks random labels; a tiny device might use a pattern instead, which is faster but could leak hints about what device it is.

sections.title: Padding, Dummy Packets, and Integrity Checks
sections.content:
Padding ensures that encrypted data aligns to block boundaries required by some encryption algorithms. A full ESP implementation includes Traffic Flow Confidentiality (TFC) padding to hide the size of encrypted messages. Minimal ESP does not implement TFC; it only applies the standard padding needed for encryption. This slightly leaks the message size, but it saves processing and energy.

ESP includes the concept of 'dummy packets'—packets with no actual payload, used for traffic shaping. A minimal implementation must be able to receive and discard dummy packets without error, but it need not generate them.

Integrity checks (ICV) are always present, but a minimal implementation can skip the detailed validation of padding format on received packets, as long as it still validates the ICV itself. The standard algorithm for generating the ICV uses a hash-based message authentication code over the packet contents.
sections.plainLanguage: Padding is filler to make the message fit the encryption block size. A full system wastes extra padding to hide message size; a minimal system does not bother. It still checks that nothing got corrupted (the integrity check), just not the padding format.

sections.title: Cryptographic Choices
sections.content:
RFC 4303 defines several encryption and authentication algorithms for ESP. A minimal implementation does not need to support all of them. Instead, it should support at least one encryption algorithm (such as AES) and one authentication algorithm (such as HMAC with a hash function).

The RFC provides recommendations on which algorithm combinations are secure and efficient. For constrained devices, the choice of algorithm significantly impacts power and performance. For example, AES-CTR (counter mode) avoids the need for padding and allows stream encryption, while AES-CBC requires padding and is slower on some platforms.

Any rekeying mechanism—replacing an old security association with a new one—is important even for constrained devices to prevent sequence numbers from rolling over and exposing cryptographic keys to excessive reuse.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption is like putting a message in a locked box. Different locks (algorithms) have different strengths and speeds. A tiny device picks one that works and is fast enough, not all of them.

sections.title: Risks and Trade-Offs
sections.content:
Skipping optional features comes with trade-offs. Omitting anti-replay protection leaves the implementation vulnerable to replay attacks, but may be acceptable if the threat model is low (for example, a temperature sensor whose repeated readings are harmless). Omitting TFC padding leaks message size, which could reveal application behavior; this is acceptable for low-risk deployments like a door sensor but not for health or financial data.

Using non-random SPIs can leak device type or firmware version. A privacy analysis should assess whether the information leaked is sensitive in the deployment context. Similarly, deriving the sequence number from time instead of a counter is secure only if the device's clock is reliable and cannot be manipulated.

Rekeying is essential: even constrained devices should rekey security associations periodically to prevent sequence number rollover and to refresh cryptographic material.
sections.plainLanguage: Skipping security checks is like not locking your door to save effort—it works if your house is in a safe neighborhood, but it is risky in others. The RFC tells you when shortcuts are safe.

sections.title: Staying Compatible with Standard ESP
sections.content:
The key requirement is that a minimal ESP implementation must not break interoperability with standard, full ESP implementations. This means the packet format must remain unchanged, the algorithms must be compatible, and the handling of valid and invalid packets must be correct.

For instance, a minimal implementation can choose not to generate dummy packets, but it must silently discard any dummy packets it receives without signaling an error. It can choose not to implement anti-replay protection, but if it receives an out-of-order packet, it must either accept it (because it does not check order) or reject it silently, not report an error that breaks the connection.

This approach allows a constrained device to implement just enough ESP to participate in an IPsec network without dragging down the entire system with features it cannot afford.
sections.plainLanguage: The tiny device does not have to do everything, but whatever it does have to be the same as what bigger systems expect. It is like a restaurant that offers fewer dishes but every dish tastes right.
